subtopics.title: UAE Visit: Strategic Outcomes
subtopics.summary: PM Modi's UAE visit produced agreements and proposals on energy security, LPG supply, shipbuilding and defence, and AI infrastructure. The energy outcomes centre on strategic crude storage and an LPG supply partnership with ADNOC. Investment interest in India's infrastructure sector was also noted.
facts: MoU between Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited and Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) for strategic collaboration.
Proposal to store up to 30 million barrels of ADNOC crude oil in India's Strategic Petroleum Reserves.
Discussions on storing crude oil in Fujairah under India's Overseas Strategic Reserve Framework.
IOCL and ADNOC signed a strategic collaboration agreement on LPG supply security; a long-term LPG sale deal between ADNOC Gas and IOCL is a potential deal.
Framework advanced for a Strategic Defence Partnership between India and the UAE.
Cochin Shipyard and Drydocks World MoU to establish a Ship Repair Cluster at Vadinar.
Cooperation includes offshore fabrication under the Maritime Development Fund Scheme.
Term sheet signed for setting up 8 Exaflop Super Computing Clusters.
Partnership between C-DAC and G42 under India's AI Mission.
Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and National Infrastructure and Investment Fund to explore investments up to US$1 billion in India's infrastructure sector.

subtopics.title: UAE: Trade, Diaspora and Country Profile
subtopics.summary: India-UAE trade in FY 2025-26 stood at US$100 billion, and the UAE is among India's largest energy suppliers and export destinations. The 2022 CEPA and the UAE's share of India's remittance flows are key economic links. The booklet also profiles the UAE's government and the Kafala sponsorship system.
facts: Trade between India and the UAE in FY 2025-26: US$100 billion.
UAE is India's 2nd largest export destination, after the US.
UAE is India's 3rd largest crude oil source.
UAE is India's 3rd largest supplier of LNG and 2nd largest supplier of LPG.
UAE is the only nation participating in India's Strategic Reserve Programme.
In 2022, India was the first country with which the UAE signed a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).
UAE accounted for 18% of India's remittance flows.
UAE is a federal, elective monarchy of 7 emirates; capital Abu Dhabi; currency dirham.
Kafala system: a sponsorship system in Gulf countries that ties a foreign worker's visa and legal status to an in-country sponsor, typically the employer.
Indian nationals form the largest expatriate community within the UAE.

subtopics.title: Norway, Nordic Group and Sweden
subtopics.summary: PM Modi made the first bilateral visit by an Indian PM to Norway in 43 years and attended the 3rd India-Nordic Summit in Oslo. Ties with Norway were upgraded to a Green Strategic Partnership, and ties with Sweden were elevated to a Strategic Partnership. The core Nordic group has five countries.
facts: PM Modi undertook the first bilateral visit by an Indian PM to Norway in 43 years.
The 3rd India-Nordic Summit was held in Oslo; earlier summits were in Stockholm (2018) and Copenhagen (2022).
India and Norway upgraded ties to a Green Strategic Partnership covering clean energy transition, climate resilience, blue economy and green shipping.
Norway formally joined India's Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative.
PM Modi was awarded Norway's highest civilian honour, the Grand Cross of the Royal Norwegian Order of Merit.
India-EFTA TEPA was signed in 2024.
Norwegian Sovereign Wealth Fund (GPFG) has invested about USD 28 billion in India.
Core Nordic countries: Denmark, Finland, Iceland (least populous), Norway and Sweden (most populous).
India and Sweden elevated ties to a Strategic Partnership and adopted the India-Sweden Joint Action Plan 2026-2030.
India and Sweden launched LeadIT at the UN Climate Action Summit in 2019 and endorsed joint development of SITAC, the India-Sweden Technology and Artificial Intelligence Corridor.

subtopics.title: Italy and Netherlands: Partnerships and Heritage
subtopics.summary: India and Italy upgraded ties to a Special Strategic Partnership, targeting EUR 20 billion in bilateral trade by 2029 and backing the IMEEC corridor. Cooperation with the Netherlands covers semiconductors, water management and the return of 11th-century Chola copper plates. The booklet also places the Afsluitdijk Dam in the Netherlands alongside the proposed Kalpasar Project in Gujarat.
facts: India and Italy upgraded bilateral relations to a Special Strategic Partnership.
India and Italy committed to raising bilateral trade to EUR 20 billion by 2029.
Both nations support IMEEC, which aims to improve trade connectivity, logistics, energy and digital links between Asia and Europe.
2027 is declared the Year of Culture and Tourism between India and Italy, marking 80 years of diplomatic relations.
Italy is India's 4th largest trading partner in the EU.
MoU between Tata Electronics and ASML supports India's semiconductor plant in Dholera, Gujarat.
Leiden University returned 11th-century Chola copper plates (Anaimangalam Copper Plates) to India.
Afsluitdijk Dam: a 32 km long barrier dam in the Netherlands that transformed the saline Zuiderzee inlet into freshwater IJsselmeer Lake.
Kalpasar Project (Gujarat): proposed dam across the Gulf of Khambhat, expected to create the world's largest freshwater reservoir.
Kalpasar objectives: freshwater storage, flood control, climate resilience, irrigation support and regional development.

topics.title: UAE's Exit from OPEC and OPEC+

subtopics.title: UAE's Exit from OPEC and OPEC+
subtopics.summary: The United Arab Emirates announced that it will leave OPEC and the wider OPEC+ alliance, effective 01 May 2026. The exit is seen as a major geopolitical shift that could weaken OPEC's influence over the global oil market. OPEC+ brings OPEC together with major non-OPEC producers, and the alliance pumps around 40% of the world's crude oil.
facts: UAE joined OPEC in 1967.
UAE's exit from OPEC and OPEC+ is effective 01 May 2026.
The exit is seen as a major geopolitical shift.
The exit could weaken OPEC's influence over the global oil market.
The exit reduces the group's collective ability to control global oil prices.
OPEC+ is an alliance of OPEC and 11 major non-OPEC producers, formed in 2016.
OPEC+ pumps around 40% of the world's crude oil.

subtopics.title: OPEC: Origin, Mandate and Membership
subtopics.summary: OPEC was established in 1960 at the Baghdad Conference and is headquartered in Vienna, Austria. Its mandate is to protect oil exporters' interests by coordinating production policies for stable supply and fair returns. It acts as a regulatory authority for the international energy market, using production quotas to prevent extreme fluctuations in crude oil prices.
facts: Established in 1960 at the Baghdad Conference.
Founding members: Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela.
Headquarters in Vienna, Austria.
Mandate: protect oil exporters' interests through coordinated production policies.
Uses production quotas to prevent extreme fluctuations in crude oil prices.
After the UAE's exit, OPEC has 11 members.
Members include Algeria, Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Libya, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela.
Ecuador suspended its membership in 1992; Gabon terminated its membership in January 1995.
All OPEC member countries are signatories to the UNFCCC.

subtopics.title: Reasons Behind the Exit and Its Impact
subtopics.summary: Production quota limits stopped the UAE from fully using its expanding oil capacity, and it aims for about 5 million barrels/day by 2027. The UAE also expects global oil demand to peak soon and then decline, so it wants strong oil revenues now while preparing for the energy transition. Long-standing tensions with Saudi Arabia over production policy add to the pressures behind the exit.
facts: Production quota constraints limited the UAE's ability to fully use its expanding oil capacity.
The UAE aims to reach about 5 million barrels/day by 2027.
The UAE holds the world's 6th largest oil reserves.
The UAE predicts an imminent peak in global oil demand, followed by gradual decline.
Strategy: maximise short-term oil revenues while preparing for a long-term transition to renewables.
Oil revenues are meant to fund AI and data centre growth, driving a diversified economy.
Long-standing tensions with Saudi Arabia over production policy within OPEC.
Independent production strategies may lead to greater price volatility.
Peak Oil Theory, proposed by M. King Hubbert, says production follows a bell-shaped curve before irreversible decline.

subtopics.title: Habshan-Fujairah Pipeline and India's Stake
subtopics.summary: The Habshan-Fujairah pipeline is a crude oil pipeline in the UAE that carries oil from inland fields to a port on the Gulf of Oman, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. It boosts UAE export flexibility, which matters amid Strait of Hormuz disruption risks. For India, lower oil prices would reduce import costs and ease inflationary pressure.
facts: Crude oil pipeline in the UAE.
Connects inland oil fields of Habshan to the port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman.
Bypasses the Strait of Hormuz.
Boosts UAE export flexibility and enables higher output amid Strait of Hormuz disruption risks.
India stands to gain from decreased oil prices.
Lower prices would reduce India's import costs and mitigate inflationary pressures.
The shift allows direct bilateral negotiations outside traditional cartel restrictions.
Supports India's de-dollarisation by encouraging energy settlements in rupees.
Heightened market volatility could complicate India's long-term energy budgeting.

subtopics.title: NEET-UG 2026 cancellation and re-test
subtopics.summary: NEET-UG 2026 was declared compromised after paper leak allegations, and the examination was officially cancelled. Reports of illicit leaks and unauthorised material on digital platforms led to an investigation, and fraudulent guess papers that closely mirrored the actual test were among the evidence. The NTA voided the initial results and ordered a re-test for all candidates without any further application cost.
facts: NEET 2026 was declared compromised amid paper leak allegations.
Official cancellation of NEET-UG 2026 was followed by a planned re-sitting.
Reports of illicit paper leaks and unauthorised exam materials on digital platforms triggered an investigation.
Fraudulent 'guess papers' that closely mirrored the actual test were part of the evidence.
NTA decided to void the initial results to maintain integrity and public trust.
The re-test is to be administered again for all candidates.
Candidates do not have to pay any further application costs for the re-test.

subtopics.title: NEET, NTA and the 2024 controversy
subtopics.summary: NEET is the National Entrance Examination for admission into medical colleges across India, and it is conducted by the National Testing Agency. The NTA was established in 2017 as an autonomous body under the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education. The NEET-UG 2024 controversy, marked by an unusually high number of full-mark scorers, led to a high-level committee headed by former ISRO Chairman Dr K Radhakrishnan.
facts: NEET is the National Entrance Examination for admission into medical colleges across India.
NEET-UG is conducted by the National Testing Agency.
The NTA was established in 2017.
The NTA is an autonomous body under the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education.
The NTA's headquarters are in New Delhi and its head is Pradeep Kumar Joshi.
The NTA also conducts JEE Main and CUET.
In 2024, an unusually high number of candidates achieved full marks.
Only two candidates secured full marks in 2023, and no candidate did in 2022.
After the NEET-UG 2024 controversy, the Ministry of Education constituted a high-level committee headed by former ISRO Chairman Dr K Radhakrishnan.

subtopics.title: Ripple effect of exam malpractice
subtopics.summary: Exam malpractice damages far more than a single examination. It lowers the value of academic credentials, adds financial burden on government institutions and erodes public trust in fairness. Students also suffer, as cancellations delay admissions and honest candidates face stress and demotivation.
facts: Loss of system credibility reduces the market value of degrees and merit rankings.
Re-conducting compromised examinations imposes a heavy financial burden on government institutions.
Large-scale cheating makes parents and students lose confidence in educational fairness.
Exam cancellations delay admissions and disrupt the academic calendar for millions of students.
Unfair practices cause significant stress, frustration and demotivation for honest candidates.
The impacts are grouped into systemic and institutional damage, and impact on students.

subtopics.title: Panel recommendations
subtopics.summary: The panel's major recommendations focus on the role of the NTA, institutional governance, secure examination centres and technology. It proposed limiting the NTA to entrance examinations for higher education institutions and creating 10 new posts. It also recommended a Digi-Yatra-like authentication system and a gradual shift to computer adaptive testing.
facts: The NTA should focus only on entrance examinations for higher education institutions, not recruitment examinations.
The panel proposed creating 10 new posts for administration, IT infrastructure and digital security.
A technology-enabled authentication system similar to Digi-Yatra was proposed under a Digi-Exam framework.
Governance reforms recommended an empowered governing body with sub-committees for test audits, ethics and transparency, and staff management and appointments.
Greater use of Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan institutions and Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya campuses as examination centres was recommended.
Gradual adoption of computer adaptive testing was proposed for future entrance examinations.

subtopics.title: Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act 2024
subtopics.summary: The Act aims to curb paper leaks, organised cheating and manipulation in recruitment and entrance examinations. It sets imprisonment of 3 to 10 years for individuals, with fines and debarment for service providers and a separate penalty for organised crime. Offences are cognisable, non-bailable and non-compoundable, and investigations can be transferred to a Central Investigating Agency.
facts: The Act's objective is to curb paper leaks, organised cheating and manipulation in recruitment and entrance examinations.
For individuals, imprisonment ranges from 3 to 10 years depending on the offence, and monetary penalties up to 1 crore apply in organised malpractice.
Service providers face a fine up to 1 crore and debarment from conducting examinations for 4 years.
Organised crimes attract imprisonment between 5 and 10 years and a minimum fine of 1 crore.
Property attachment and forfeiture are possible for organised crimes.
Offences under the Act are cognisable, non-bailable and non-compoundable.
Investigations are conducted by officers not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police or Assistant Commissioner of Police.
The Central Government may transfer investigations to a Central Investigating Agency when required.

subtopics.title: Madhya Pradesh High Court Judgment
subtopics.summary: The Madhya Pradesh High Court declared the Bhojshala - Kamal Maula Complex a Hindu temple and quashed the 2003 ASI order that allowed shared worship. It held that the Places of Worship Act, 1991 did not apply because the site is a protected monument. The court also directed the State Government to consider alternative land in Dhar for a mosque or prayer site.
facts: The MP High Court declared the complex a Hindu temple of Goddess Vagdevi (Saraswati), based on 2024 ASI survey findings.
The court quashed the 2003 ASI order that had allowed shared worship at the site.
The Places of Worship Act, 1991 was held inapplicable because the site falls under the AMASR Act, 1958 as a protected monument.
Section 4(3) of the Places of Worship Act excludes ancient monuments under the AMASR Act, 1958 from the religious character freeze.
The Muslim side's reliance on an August 1935 proclamation by the princely State of Dhar was rejected.
The Government of India Act, 1935 was not enforced until April 1937.
The case was treated as a Writ Petition under Article 226 seeking enforcement of the fundamental right to worship.
Unlike the Babri Masjid dispute (a Title Suit over ownership), the Bhojshala case was a writ petition.
The State Government was directed to consider allotting alternative land within Dhar for a mosque or prayer site.

subtopics.title: Places of Worship Act, 1991
subtopics.summary: The Places of Worship Act, 1991 freezes the religious character of places of worship as it stood on 15 August 1947 and prohibits their conversion. It terminates pre-1947 disputes, allows new cases only for post-1947 changes, and provides penalties for violations. The Act has drawn criticism on grounds of judicial review, federalism, equality and the 1947 cut-off date.
facts: The Act was passed by the P V Narasimha Rao-led Congress government.
Section 3 prohibits converting a place of worship between or within religious denominations.
Section 4(1) ensures the religious identity of a place of worship remains as it was on August 15, 1947.
Section 4(2) terminates legal proceedings on pre-1947 religious character conversions; new cases are allowed only for post-1947 changes.
Section 5 provides exceptions for ancient monuments under the AMASR Act, 1958 and for the Ayodhya dispute.
Section 6 provides penalties with a maximum imprisonment term of 3 years, along with fines.
Critics say the Act bars judicial review, limiting constitutional checks and balances.
Critics say the Act violates the right to religion (Art 25-28) and undermines equality (Art 14-15).
Critics say the August 15, 1947 cut-off ignores historical injustices and pre-1947 encroachments.
The Supreme Court's 2019 Ayodhya verdict said the Act upholds secular values and prohibits retrogression.

subtopics.title: Historical and Religious Claims
subtopics.summary: The site is a medieval ASI-protected monument in Dhar, Madhya Pradesh, traditionally linked to Raja Bhoj, who built it in 1034 AD. Hindus regard it as a Saraswati temple, while Muslims identify it as the Kamal Maula Mosque. It was reportedly converted into a mosque in 1514 AD, and an idol of Goddess Saraswati found at the site is now in the British Museum, London.
facts: Medieval ASI-protected monument located in Dhar, Madhya Pradesh.
Hindus claim the site as a Saraswati temple; Muslims consider it a mosque.
Built by Raja Bhoj in 1034 AD.
The term 'Bhojshala' became linked to the building in the early 20th century, based on inscriptions found at the site by KK Lele.
The structure is believed to have originally functioned as a temple dedicated to Goddess Saraswati (Vagdevi).
Reportedly converted into a mosque in 1514 AD under Muslim rule (Mehmudshah Khilji) in Dhar.
Muslims identify the structure as the Kamal Maula Mosque, associated with Sufi saint Hazrat Maulana Kamaluddin Chishti.
An intricately carved idol of Goddess Saraswati was discovered at the site during excavations in the 20th century.
The Saraswati idol is currently housed in the British Museum, London.
The site was traditionally regarded as a centre of Sanskrit learning and scholarship.

subtopics.title: Architecture, Inscriptions and Gurjara-Pratihara Links
subtopics.summary: The complex preserves the remains of a Mandapa-style hall, typical of Hindu temple architecture, and two Sarpabandha pillar inscriptions that teach Sanskrit grammar. Its walls carry odes to Kurma Avatara in Prakrit, and its inscriptions mention Paramara rulers. Raja Bhoj, recognized as Mihir Bhoja, is linked to the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire.
facts: Structural remains indicate a Mandapa-style hall, characteristic of Hindu temple architecture.
The site uniquely preserves 2 Sarpabandha (serpentine chart) pillar inscriptions.
The Sarpabandha inscriptions chart the Sanskrit alphabet, noun/verb terminations, and the ten tenses and moods of Sanskrit grammar.
Stone slabs on the walls carry two odes to Kurma Avatara (Tortoise Incarnation of Vishnu), composed in Prakrit.
Sanskrit and Pali inscriptions mention Paramara rulers such as Udayaditya, Naravarman and Arjunavarma Deva.
The Sanskrit drama Karpuramanjari was written by royal tutor Madana, a disciple of Jain scholar Ashadhara.
Gurjara-Pratihara Empire founder: Nagabhata I (730-756 AD).
Raja Bhoj (Mihir Bhoja) was the most illustrious emperor of the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire.
Capital of the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire: Kannauj (Mahodaya).
The Pratiharas were central to a tripartite struggle against the Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan.

topics.title: Increase in Supreme Court Judge Strength

subtopics.title: Expansion Bill and Legal Framework
subtopics.summary: The Union Cabinet approved the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill 2026 to expand the Court to 38 judges, which is the Chief Justice plus 37 other judges. Article 124 empowers Parliament to change the number of judges by law, and the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956 governs this. The Court was inaugurated in 1950 and succeeded the Federal Court of India.
facts: Cabinet approved the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill 2026
Proposed strength is 38 judges (CJI plus 37 other judges)
Article 124 empowers Parliament to increase judges by law
Governed by the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956
Increase needs an Amendment Bill passed by both Houses
Simple majority is sufficient; Presidential assent is also needed
Inaugurated on 28 January 1950
Succeeded the Federal Court of India (Government of India Act, 1935)
Replaced the British Privy Council as the highest court of appeal
Originally fixed at 8 (Chief Justice and 7 other judges)

subtopics.title: Qualifications, Tenure and Removal
subtopics.summary: Judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President, subject to qualifications set in the Constitution. A judge holds office until the age of 65 and may resign by writing to the President. Removal is only on grounds of proven misbehaviour or incapacity, under the Judges Enquiry Act, 1968, and needs a Parliamentary vote.
facts: Judges are appointed by the President
Must be a citizen of India
Five years as a High Court judge is one qualification route
A Distinguished Jurist in the President's opinion is another route
No fixed tenure; holds office until 65 years of age
A judge may resign by writing to the President
Removal only on proven misbehaviour or incapacity
Removal by the President on Parliament's recommendation
Judges Enquiry Act, 1968 governs the removal procedure for SC and HC judges
Justice Soumitra Sen (2011) resigned before Lok Sabha discussion

subtopics.title: CJI Appointment Convention and Collegium
subtopics.summary: Until 1973 the seniormost judge was normally appointed Chief Justice of India, a convention that was broken in 1973 and 1977. The Second Judges Case (1993) ruled that only the seniormost judge should be appointed CJI and that consultation means concurrence. The 2015 Fourth Judges Case struck down the NJAC and the 99th Amendment.
facts: Till 1973, the seniormost judge was normally appointed CJI
1973: AN Ray appointed CJI, superseding JM Shelat, KS Hegde and AN Grover
1977: MU Beg appointed CJI, superseding HR Khanna
1981 (First Judges Case): consultation only implies exchange of views
1993 (Second Judges Case): consultation changed to mean concurrence
1993: only the seniormost judge should be appointed CJI
1998 (Third Judges Case): CJI must consult a collegium of 4 seniormost judges
1998: if 2 judges give an adverse opinion, no recommendation is sent
2015 (Fourth Judges Case): 99th Amendment and NJAC Act declared void
NJAC: CJI chairperson, 2 seniormost judges, Law Minister, 2 eminent persons

subtopics.title: Jurisdiction and Temporary Appointments
subtopics.summary: The Supreme Court has appellate, original and advisory jurisdiction. Article 32 allows direct approach for violation of Fundamental Rights, while the President can seek an advisory opinion under Article 143 that is not binding. Articles 126, 127 and 128 allow an Acting CJI, ad hoc judges and retired judges in specified situations.
facts: Appellate jurisdiction covers appeals against lower court judgments
Appeals from High Courts need a certificate under Article 134A
Article 131 gives original jurisdiction in certain disputes
Article 32: direct approach for violation of Fundamental Rights
Article 143: President may seek advisory opinion on public importance questions
Advisory opinion is NOT binding on the President
Article 126: Acting CJI appointed when CJI post is vacant or absent
Article 127: CJI can appoint a High Court judge as ad hoc judge for lack of quorum
Article 127 needs prior consent of the President
Article 128: retired SC or HC judge can be requested to sit, with consent

subtopics.title: Origin and Objective
subtopics.summary: The Anti-Defection Law was introduced through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985, and placed in the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution. Its objective is to prevent political defections and ensure stability in governments. The phrase 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' is linked to frequent party-switching by legislators in the 1960s. The law applies to both Parliament and State Assemblies.
facts: Introduced through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985
Enshrined in the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution
Objective: prevent political defections and ensure stability in governments
Phrase 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' linked to frequent party-switching in the 1960s
Applies to both Parliament and State Legislatures
Constitutional basis: Articles 102(1) and 191(1)
Lays down the process for disqualifying legislators on grounds of defection

subtopics.title: Grounds for Disqualification
subtopics.summary: A legislator loses membership if they voluntarily give up party membership or vote or abstain contrary to the party whip. Under Articles 102(1) and 191(1), a legislator can also be disqualified for holding an office of profit, being declared of unsound mind by a court, being an undischarged insolvent, losing Indian citizenship or showing allegiance to another country, or being disqualified under any law made by Parliament. The booklet also lists joining another party and opposing party direction as grounds in the disqualification summary.
facts: Voluntarily giving up party membership is a ground for disqualification
Voting or abstaining contrary to the party whip is a ground for disqualification
Holding an office of profit is a ground under Articles 102(1) and 191(1)
Being declared of unsound mind by a court is a ground
Being an undischarged insolvent is a ground
Losing Indian citizenship or showing allegiance to another country is a ground
Disqualification under any law made by Parliament is a ground

subtopics.title: Exceptions, Mergers and Member Categories
subtopics.summary: A party can merge without disqualification if two-thirds of the members of a legislature party agree, a provision retained after the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003. That amendment removed the earlier split provision, under which one-third of members could split without disqualification. A whip breach is excused if prior permission is taken or the party condones the action within 15 days. Independent members are disqualified for joining a party after election, while nominated members are disqualified for joining after six months of nomination.
facts: Merger: no disqualification if two-thirds of a legislature party agree to merge
Earlier, one-third of members could split without disqualification
The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act (2003) removed the split provision
Whip exception: prior permission taken, or party condones the action within 15 days
Independent member: disqualified if they join a party after election
Nominated member: disqualified if they join a party after six months of nomination
Merger provision is an exception to disqualification under the law

subtopics.title: Deciding Authority and Judicial Review
subtopics.summary: The Speaker (Lok Sabha) or the Chairman (Rajya Sabha) decides disqualification petitions, and the decision is subject to judicial review. Keisham Meghachandra Singh vs Speaker Manipur (2020) says such decisions should ideally be made within 3 months. The grounds for reviewing a Speaker's decision, laid down in Shrimanth Balasaheb Patil vs Speaker Karnataka (2019), include violation of a constitutional mandate, malafide intent, a perverse decision, and failure to follow natural justice.
facts: Speaker (Lok Sabha) or Chairman (Rajya Sabha) decides disqualification
Decision of the Speaker or Chairman is subject to judicial review
Kihoto Hollohan vs Zachillhu (1992): Speaker's decisions subject to judicial review
Keisham Meghachandra Singh vs Speaker Manipur (2020): decisions ideally within 3 months
Shrimanth Balasaheb Patil vs Speaker Karnataka (2019): review grounds include malafide intent and perverse decision
Ravi S Naik vs Union of India: membership can be inferred from members' conduct

subtopics.title: Significance, Criticisms and Key Issues
subtopics.summary: The law allows party mergers without disqualifying members, prevents defections for office or material gain, and supports party stability and discipline. Critics point to long delays in deciding disqualification petitions, allegations that presiding officers act partisanly, and limited judicial intervention before the Speaker decides. They also argue that the two-thirds merger clause enables mass defections and that the rigid whip system reduces intra-party democracy.
facts: Prevents defections for office or material gain
Ensures party stability and prevents government instability
Ensures party discipline through adherence to the whip
Makes legislators accountable for their conduct
Key issue: disqualification petitions often remain pending for long durations
Key issue: allegations of bias, as Speaker or Chairman may act partisanly
Key issue: courts typically intervene only after the Speaker's decision
Key issue: rigid whip system, including whips on non-critical matters
Key issue: two-thirds merger clause enables large-scale defections

topics.title: India's Forex Stress and Call for Economic Austerity

subtopics.title: Forex Reserves: Decline and Role
subtopics.summary: India's forex reserves fell by nearly USD 38 billion within two months, reaching around USD 691 billion by May 2026. The reserves are external assets held by the RBI and act as a buffer against external shocks. They strengthen when inflows exceed outflows and weaken when outflows rise.
facts: Reserves declined by nearly USD 38 billion within two months, to about USD 691 billion by May 2026
Three triggers cited: volatile oil prices, record-breaking gold imports, RBI intervention to defend the rupee
Forex reserves are external assets maintained by the Reserve Bank of India
Components: foreign currency assets, gold reserves, Special Drawing Rights, reserve position with the IMF
Inflows exceeding outflows strengthen reserves and support rupee stability
Rising outflows or falling foreign investment can reduce reserves and depreciate the rupee
Reserves ensure uninterrupted access to crude oil, fertilisers and industrial machinery
Reserves act as a shield against global instability and sudden capital outflows
Lower reserves mean a reduced buffer and higher sensitivity to global capital flows

subtopics.title: Import Pressures: Oil, Gold and Fertiliser
subtopics.summary: India's current account deficit is widened by heavy reliance on imported crude oil, record gold purchases and costly fertiliser inputs. Each of these imports draws on dollar reserves and adds pressure on the rupee. The booklet links this to a persistent CAD and imported inflation.
facts: India imports around 89% of its crude oil requirement
Every USD 1 rise in oil price adds USD 1.5 to 2 billion to the import bill
India is the 2nd largest gold consumer globally, after China
Gold accounts for nearly USD 72 billion, about 9% of total imports
Household gold imports do not add to productive capacity and directly worsen the CAD
Imported inputs such as urea and ammonia prices have doubled
Oil marketing companies face under-recoveries because retail fuel prices are frozen
Rupee depreciation raises import costs, which push up domestic prices
Persistent CAD reflects inelastic import demand and dependence on external financing

subtopics.title: Why the Government Seeks Austerity
subtopics.summary: The Prime Minister has urged citizens to limit non-essential spending on gold, overseas travel and fuel. The aims are to manage the CAD, stabilise the rupee and contain capital flight. The approach shifts from supply-side diversification to demand-side restraint.
facts: PM urged citizens to reduce non-essential spending on gold, overseas travel and fuel
Cutting non-essential imports helps conserve foreign exchange
Demand-side measures include work-from-home, carpooling and virtual meetings
Surging fertiliser prices push government to prioritise food security over discretionary fuel use
Austerity aims to curb capital flight and reduce forex outflows
Strategic autonomy: shift from supply-side diversification to demand-side restraint
Goal: reduce dependence on volatile regions and lower energy-to-GDP sensitivity
Aim: strengthen resilience against global shocks

subtopics.title: Costs of Excessive Forex Conservation
subtopics.summary: The booklet cautions that overly strict controls could stifle manufacturing, weaken exports and discourage foreign investment. Suppressing private consumption also threatens aggregate demand and job creation. Past import-substitution attempts are cited as a warning, since they led to low competitiveness.
facts: Indian industry depends on imported capital goods, semiconductors and raw materials
Restricted imports lower industrial output and exports
Protectionism trap: import curbs raise input costs and reduce export competitiveness
Capital control concerns raise the country risk premium
Foreign direct and portfolio investment inflows could be dampened
Private consumption is a major GDP component; reducing it weakens growth
Foreign investors avoid economies lacking strong domestic demand
Past import-substitution efforts led to low industrial competitiveness and inefficiency
Lower production leads to significantly reduced job creation

subtopics.title: Index Overview and Methodology
subtopics.summary: The World Press Freedom Index is an annual report published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), a non-profit organisation with headquarters in Paris. It has been published annually since 2002, and the 2026 edition is the 24th. The Index ranks 180 countries and regions on the level of freedom available to journalists, using a Press Freedom Questionnaire with five categories. Each country receives a score from 0 (worst) to 100 (best).
facts: Published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), a non-profit organisation
RSF was founded in 1985 and has its headquarters in Paris, France
Annual report since 2002; the 2026 edition is the 24th
Ranks 180 countries and regions by freedom available to journalists
Evaluates pluralism, media independence, legal framework and journalist safety
Press Freedom Questionnaire covers 5 categories
Each country gets a score from 0 (worst) to 100 (best)
Aim: safeguarding the right to freedom of information

subtopics.title: Key Findings and Country Rankings 2026
subtopics.summary: The 2026 Index finds that global press freedom has declined, with 52.2 per cent of countries rated 'Difficult' or 'Very Serious' for journalism. Only 1 per cent of the world's population lives in countries rated 'Good'. Norway remains top-ranked, while Syria recorded the sharpest rise after its political transition and Niger the steepest fall. The Middle East and North Africa remained the most dangerous region for journalists.
facts: Global press freedom declines; a majority of countries (52.2%) face Difficult or Very Serious conditions
Only 1% of the population lives in countries rated 'Good' for journalism
Norway is top-ranked for the 10th consecutive year, with a score of 92.72
Top-ranked order: Norway, Netherlands, Estonia, Denmark, Sweden
Netherlands scored 88.92 and was ranked second on the score list
Bottom-ranked countries named: Eritrea, North Korea, China, Iran, Saudi Arabia
Legal indicator saw the sharpest decline, due to criminalisation of journalism and misuse of laws
Middle East and North Africa remained the most dangerous region for journalists
Syria rose sharply in rankings after its political transition
Niger suffered the steepest ranking fall (120th) due to military rule and armed group violence in the Sahel
India ranked 157th with a score of 31.96 ('Very Serious') in 2026, from 151st in 2025

subtopics.title: Challenges and Significance of a Free Press
subtopics.summary: Media in 160 of the 180 countries face financial instability, which threatens independent and unbiased reporting, and political instability is linked to declining media freedom. A free press is often described as the fourth pillar of democracy, giving voice to marginalised communities and sparking debate that can lead to reform. During the pandemic, media acted as a critical communication tool between governments and citizens. Under the Indian Constitution, press freedom flows from Article 19(1)(a) but remains subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).
facts: Media in 160 of 180 countries face financial instability
Political instability is linked to decline in media freedom
Press is often called the 4th pillar of democracy, alongside legislature, judiciary and executive
Press acts as a bridge between the governed and the governing, especially for marginalised communities
Press sparks public debate, a precursor to legislative and social reform
During the pandemic, media was a critical communication tool between government and citizens
Freedom of press is treated as part of freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a)
Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions, including on defamation, contempt of court and public order
Freedom of media is not an absolute freedom
In Romesh Thappar vs State of Madras (1950), the Supreme Court said freedom of press lies at the foundation of all democratic organisations

subtopics.title: History and Institutions of Press Freedom in India
subtopics.summary: Printing in India expanded under European trading companies, and India's first newspaper, the Bengal Gazette, appeared in 1780. Colonial measures such as the Censorship of Press Act 1799 and the Vernacular Press Act 1878 restricted the press, while Metcalfe's Press Act 1835 is remembered as the liberator of the Indian press. Today, the Press Council of India, set up under the Press Council Act 1978, and the Editors Guild of India work to uphold press freedom and journalistic standards.
facts: East India Company set up its first printing press in Bombay in 1674
James Augustus Hickey's Bengal Gazette, India's first newspaper, was published in 1780
Censorship of Press Act 1799, issued by Lord Wellesley, curbed French propaganda against British rule
Raja Rammohan Roy founded the Bengali weekly Sambad Kaumudi (1821) to champion social reform
Bombay Samachar (1822), India's oldest running vernacular newspaper, was founded by Fardoonji Murazban
Metcalfe's Press Act 1835 is known as the liberator of the Indian press
Vernacular Press Act 1878, proposed by Lord Lytton, was enacted to suppress press freedom and criticism of British rule
Press Council of India was initially established in 1966 under the Indian Press Council Act 1965
Press Council of India was abolished in 1975 during the Emergency, after repeal of the 1965 Act
Press Council of India was established in 1978 as a statutory quasi-judicial body under the Press Council Act 1978

subtopics.title: LEADS Index Basics
subtopics.summary: LEADS stands for Logistics Ease Across Different States and is India's national index for benchmarking logistics performance across States and UTs. It was launched in 2018 and draws inspiration from the World Bank's Logistics Performance Index. The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade prepares the report, and the 7th LEADS 2025 Report introduced a four-tier classification in place of the earlier three-tier model.
facts: LEADS stands for Logistics Ease Across Different States.
LEADS is India's national index benchmarking logistics performance across States and UTs.
LEADS was launched in 2018.
LEADS draws inspiration from the World Bank's Logistics Performance Index.
The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (Ministry of Commerce and Industry) prepares the LEADS Report.
The Department released the 7th LEADS 2025 Report.
The LEADS 2025 edition introduced a four-tier classification replacing the earlier three-tier model.
States and UTs are evaluated across key logistics parameters, including infrastructure, service quality, regulatory environment and data-driven logistics reforms.
The LEADS 2025 Report is presented across 13 logistics-related categories.
LEAPS stands for Logistics Excellence, Advancement and Performance Shield.

subtopics.title: State and UT Categories in LEADS 2025
subtopics.summary: The LEADS 2025 edition sorts States and UTs into four categories: Exemplars, High Performers, Accelerators and Growth-Seekers. Each entry carries a regional tag of Coastal, Landlocked, North-East (N-E) or UTs. Uttar Pradesh became an Exemplar after being an Achiever from 2022 to 2024, and Jammu and Kashmir moved from Fast Mover to High Performer.
facts: The 2025 edition introduced four new categories: Exemplars, High Performers, Accelerators and Growth-Seekers.
Exemplars (4): Tamil Nadu (Coastal), Uttar Pradesh (Landlocked), Mizoram (N-E) and Delhi (UTs).
Uttar Pradesh achieved Exemplar status after being categorised as an Achiever from 2022 to 2024.
High Performers (11): Gujarat (Coastal), Haryana (Landlocked), Tripura (N-E) and Jammu and Kashmir (UTs).
Jammu and Kashmir improved from Fast Mover in 2024 to High Performer in 2025.
Accelerators (17) include Andhra Pradesh (Coastal), Punjab (Landlocked) and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu (UTs).
Growth-Seekers (4): West Bengal (Coastal), Rajasthan (Landlocked), Sikkim (N-E) and Andaman and Nicobar Islands (UTs).
The regional tags used in the report are Coastal, Landlocked, N-E (North-East) and UTs.

subtopics.title: National Logistics Initiatives and the World Bank LPI
subtopics.summary: Several national programmes aim to strengthen logistics, including the National Logistics Policy 2022, PM GatiShakti, Bharatmala Pariyojana, Sagarmala and the E-Way Bill System. India's logistics performance is also tracked globally through the World Bank's Logistics Performance Index. That index has six key dimensions and is reported by the World Bank every two years.
facts: The National Logistics Policy 2022 aims to lower the cost of logistics to par with other developed countries.
Logistics costs in India remain relatively high at around 7.97% of GDP.
The PM GatiShakti National Master Plan 2021 promotes integrated planning across roads, railways, ports, airports and logistics networks.
The Logistic Efficiency Enhancement Programme aims to enhance freight speed, reduce costs and improve tracking.
Bharatmala Pariyojana aims to improve road connectivity across India.
The Sagarmala Programme focuses on port-led development and boosts coastal shipping efficiency.
The E-Way Bill System mandates digital bills for goods, easing inter-state transport.
The Logistics Performance Index has six key dimensions, including customs performance, infrastructure quality and timeliness of shipments.
India ranked 38th among 139 countries in the World Bank's Logistics Performance Index 2023.
The World Bank reports the Logistics Performance Index every 2 years.

subtopics.title: Dedicated Freight Corridors
subtopics.summary: Dedicated Freight Corridors are exclusive freight tracks, implemented under the Ministry of Railways by DFCCIL, that use double-stack and heavy-haul trains for high capacity and speed. They aim to reduce logistics costs, have improved port access and have contributed to Indian Railways' revenue growth. Under the National Rail Plan they are expected to raise rail's share of freight, while delays in the Western corridor added to project costs.
facts: Dedicated Freight Corridors (DFCs) are exclusive freight tracks that support double-stack and heavy-haul trains with high capacity and speed.
DFCs fall under the Ministry of Railways, and the Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India (DFCCIL) is the implementing agency.
A key objective of DFCs is to reduce logistics costs below 10% as per the National Logistics Policy.
The Western Dedicated Freight Corridor (WDFC) has improved port access and lowered transit times.
DFCs have generated jobs, attracted investments and aided economic growth.
DFCs have contributed to Indian Railways' revenue growth for FY 2018-19 to FY 2022-23.
Under the National Rail Plan, DFCs aim to boost rail freight's share to 45% by 2030.
The North-South DFC runs from Vijayawada to Itarsi and is 975 km long.
The East Coast DFC runs from Kharagpur to Vijayawada and is 1115 km long.
Delays in completing the final section of the WDFC added to project costs.

subtopics.title: Origin and observance of National Technology Day
subtopics.summary: National Technology Day is observed on 11 May each year. It was declared by PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee in 1998 to commemorate technological achievements of 11 May 1998, and has been observed annually from 1999 onward. The 2026 observance carried the theme 'Responsible Innovation for Inclusive Growth'.
facts: National Technology Day is observed on 11 May every year.
PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee declared 11 May as National Technology Day in 1998.
It has been observed annually as National Technology Day from 1999 onward.
It commemorates major technological achievements of 11 May 1998.
The 2026 observance theme was 'Responsible Innovation for Inclusive Growth'.
On 11 May 1998, Pokhran-II nuclear tests (Operation Shakti) were conducted.
On the same day, Hansa-3 completed its first successful test flight.
On the same day, DRDO successfully test-fired the Trishul short-range surface-to-air missile.
Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar awards are announced annually on National Technology Day.

subtopics.title: Pokhran nuclear tests (1974 and 1998)
subtopics.summary: India conducted a series of nuclear tests at the Pokhran Test Range in Rajasthan's Thar Desert in May 1998, under the codename Shakti. The series began on 11 May with three tests and was followed on 13 May by two more. These were the first confirmed nuclear detonations since the 1974 Pokhran-I test, codenamed 'Smiling Buddha'.
facts: Pokhran-I, India's first nuclear test, was conducted on 18 May 1974.
Pokhran-I was codenamed 'Smiling Buddha'.
Pokhran-II was a series of nuclear tests conducted by India in May 1998 at Pokhran Test Range.
The Pokhran Test Range is in Rajasthan's Thar Desert.
On 11 May 1998, India conducted three nuclear tests under the codename Shakti.
On 13 May 1998, India conducted two more nuclear tests.
Pokhran-II marked India's first confirmed nuclear detonations since the 1974 'Peaceful Nuclear Explosion'.
Operation Shakti marks India's emergence as a nuclear weapons state.
India became the 6th country to join the nuclear club.
Abdul Kalam and R. Chidambaram were the chief coordinators of Pokhran-II.

subtopics.title: Space and defence milestones
subtopics.summary: India's space and defence milestones include lunar, Mars and solar missions, along with indigenous naval and air platforms. Chandrayaan-3 achieved a soft landing near the Moon's South Pole, a global first. Upcoming missions include Gaganyaan (2027) as the first crewed spaceflight and Shukrayaan (2028) as a Venus orbiter.
facts: Chandrayaan-1 (2008) was India's first lunar mission and discovered water on the Moon.
Mangalyaan (2013) was India's first successful Mars mission, achieved on its first attempt.
In 2017, 104 satellites were launched in one launch, a world record.
Chandrayaan-3 (2023) achieved a soft landing near the Moon's South Pole, a global first.
Aditya-L1 (2023) is India's first solar mission.
Gaganyaan (2027) is the upcoming first crewed spaceflight.
Shukrayaan (2028) is the upcoming Venus Orbiter Mission.
INS Kalvari (1967) was India's first indigenous submarine.
INS Arihant is India's first ballistic missile nuclear submarine.
INS Vikrant (2022) is India's first indigenous aircraft carrier.
Tejas (LCA) is an indigenous supersonic fighter jet.

subtopics.title: Digital, farm and ranking milestones
subtopics.summary: The day also highlights India's digital infrastructure and farm milestones. Aadhaar and UPI are cited as major digital achievements, while the Green and White Revolutions transformed agriculture and dairy. India's standing in the Global Innovation Index 2026 and other rankings completes the picture.
facts: Aadhaar is the world's largest biometric ID system.
UPI (Unified Payments Interface) revolutionised digital payments.
The Green Revolution boosted production with high-yielding wheat and rice varieties.
The White Revolution made India the world's largest milk producer.
India was ranked 38th globally in the Global Innovation Index 2026.
India holds 6th position worldwide in intellectual property filings (WIPO report).
India ranks as the 3rd largest startup ecosystem globally.

subtopics.title: Institutions, schemes and awards
subtopics.summary: Several bodies and schemes support technology in India. The Technology Development Board is a statutory body that promotes the commercialisation of indigenous technology. The Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar awards, India's science honours, are announced on National Technology Day.
facts: The Technology Development Board is a statutory body under the Technology Development Board Act, 1995.
The TDB promotes development and commercialisation of indigenous technology.
The TDB also supports adaptation of imported technology for wider application.
The TDB provides financial assistance to commercialise indigenous technologies.
Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar is India's science honour, comparable to the Padma Awards.
Atal Innovation Mission, launched by NITI Aayog, fosters an innovation culture.
Atal Tinkering Labs are innovation labs in schools; Atal Incubation Centres support startups.
NM-ICPS promotes R&D in AI, Robotics, IoT, Quantum Computing and related fields.
The National Quantum Mission focuses on quantum computing, communication, sensing and materials.
iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence) promotes indigenous defence startups and MSMEs.

subtopics.title: Origin of International Labour Day
subtopics.summary: International Labour Day, also called Workers Day or May Day, is observed every year on May 1 to honour the contribution of workers. Its origin is traced to the late 19th century labour movement in the United States, where workers demanded an eight-hour working day. A large 1886 demonstration in Chicago went out of hand, and the incident known as the Haymarket Affair marked the start of the day. In 1889, Socialist Parties in Europe decided to celebrate May 1 as International Labour Day.
facts: Observed annually on May 1
Also known as Workers Day or May Day
Origin traced to the late 19th century labour movement in the United States
1886: large demonstration in America demanded 8 hours of work on a daily basis
The 1886 demonstration went out of hand in Chicago and many people got hurt
The incident is known as the Haymarket Affair
Haymarket Affair marked the start of International Labour Day
1889: Socialist Parties in Europe decided to celebrate May 1 as International Labour Day
1923: first May Day in India celebrated in Chennai (then Madras)
The 1923 celebration was by the Labour Kisan Party of Hindustan

subtopics.title: Constitutional provisions and labour laws
subtopics.summary: The Constitution gives citizens the right to form associations or unions and prohibits forced labour and employment of children below 14 years. Articles 39(a), 41, 43 and 43A set out goals for the State on livelihood, work, a living wage and worker participation in management. Labour legislation includes laws on factories, wages, provident funds and industrial disputes. Four labour codes together amalgamate 29 laws.
facts: Article 19(1)(c): right to form associations or unions
Article 23: prohibits forced labour
Article 24: prohibits employment of children below 14 years
Article 39(a): equal right to an adequate means of livelihood
Article 41: right to work and education within limits of economic capacity
Article 43: living wage, decent conditions of work, social and cultural opportunities
Article 43A: participation of workers in management of industries through legislation
Factories Act 1948; Minimum Wages Act 1948; Payment of Wages Act 1936; Workmen's Compensation Act 1923
Employees' Provident Fund Act 1952; Industrial Disputes Act 1947; Contract Labour Act 1970
Four codes amalgamate 29 laws in total: Wage Code 4, Industrial Relations Code 3, Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 13, Social Security Code 9

subtopics.title: International Labour Organisation: profile
subtopics.summary: The International Labour Organisation is a specialised agency of the United Nations dedicated to improving labour conditions and living standards throughout the world. It was established under the Treaty of Versailles and became the first specialised agency associated with the UN in 1946. Its tripartite structure gives an equal voice to governments, employers and workers. The ILO was awarded the Nobel Prize for Peace in 1969, and its headquarters is in Geneva, Switzerland.
facts: Specialised agency of the United Nations
Dedicated to improving labour conditions and living standards throughout the world
Established under the Treaty of Versailles
Became the first specialised agency associated with the UN in 1946, after the demise of the League of Nations
Tripartite structure: equal voice for governments, employers and workers
India is one of the founding members
Awarded the Nobel Prize for Peace in 1969
Director General: Gilbert Houngbo
Headquarters: Geneva, Switzerland

subtopics.title: ILO objectives, standards and reports
subtopics.summary: The ILO pursues four stated objectives: promoting fundamental labour rights, creating greater opportunities for women and men, enhancing social protection, and strengthening social dialogue and tripartism. Its international labour standards are Conventions and Protocols, which are legally binding treaties, and Recommendations, which are non-binding guidelines. The ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work, adopted in 1998, names focus areas such as freedom of association and abolition of child labour. The ILO also publishes key reports, including the Global Wage Report.
facts: Objective: promote and realise standard fundamental labour rights
Objective: create greater opportunities for women and men
Objective: enhance social protection
Objective: strengthen social dialogue and tripartism
Conventions and Protocols: legally binding international treaties
Recommendations: non-binding guidelines

Focus areas: freedom of association, elimination of forced labour, abolition of child labour, elimination of employment discrimination, safe and healthy working conditions
Fundamental conventions listed include Minimum Age (No. 138) and Freedom of Association (No. 87)
Key reports include World Employment and Social Outlook, Global Wage Report, World Social Protection Report and World of Work Report

subtopics.title: India's Partnerships: Vietnam, New Zealand and SAARC
subtopics.summary: India and Vietnam raised their ties to an enhanced Comprehensive Strategic Partnership after a state visit by To Lam, with a target of USD 25 billion bilateral trade by 2030. India and New Zealand signed a free trade agreement that eliminates duties on Indian exports to New Zealand. The SAARC currency swap framework, launched by the RBI in 2012, offers short-term liquidity support to member nations.
facts: India and Vietnam elevated ties to an enhanced Comprehensive Strategic Partnership after a state visit by To Lam
Target: USD 25 billion bilateral trade by 2030
Vietnam formally joined the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative
Joint Vision Statement for 2030 seeks deeper defence cooperation and joint development of advanced defence platforms

India gives access to 70.03% of tariff lines and keeps 29.97% under exclusion
New Zealand to invest USD 20 billion over 15 years
SAARC currency swap: central banks exchange domestic currencies at a predetermined rate and reverse the swap at the same rate
SAARC swap tenure is 3 months, extendable twice; launched by RBI in 2012

subtopics.title: ASEAN: Structure, Principles and Forums
subtopics.summary: ASEAN was formed on 8 August 1967 and is headquartered in Jakarta, with 11 members now including Timor-Leste. It works on three principles: non-interference, consensual decision-making and centrality in regional matters, and its Charter took effect in 2008. The group runs several forums and economic pacts, and India's Act East Policy places ASEAN at the centre of its Indo-Pacific vision.
facts: Formed on 8 August 1967 at Bangkok, Thailand; headquarters in Jakarta, Indonesia
11 members, including Timor-Leste (2025)
Core aims: accelerate economic and social progress, promote regional peace and stability, foster collaboration, cooperate with global organisations

East Asia Summit created in 2005 as a leaders-level forum with a varied agenda

ASEAN Economic Community formed in 2015 to facilitate free flow of goods, services, investments, capital and labour
RCEP concluded in 2019, covering 30% of the world's population

subtopics.title: Global Issues: Thucydides Trap, Ebola and Ecocide
subtopics.summary: The Thucydides Trap describes the heightened risk of conflict when a rising power challenges an established power, and it is often applied to China and the United States. WHO declared an Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, linked to the Bundibugyo strain. Ecocide refers to unlawful or reckless acts that cause severe environmental damage, and it is not currently recognised under the Rome Statute.
facts: The Thucydides Trap idea originates from Thucydides' account of the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta
Core argument: growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta made conflict increasingly inevitable
The trap describes a heightened risk of conflict when a rising power challenges an established power
Critics argue the idea oversimplifies by implying conflict is unavoidable; diplomacy and economic interdependence can prevent escalation
WHO declared the DR Congo Ebola outbreak a PHEIC, linked to the Bundibugyo strain in the Ituri region
Under the IHR 2005, a PHEIC is a public health risk of international disease spread requiring coordinated global response
Ebola is a zoonotic, severe and fatal viral disease, first identified in 1976
Ecocide: unlawful or reckless acts committed knowing they are likely to cause severe, widespread or long-term environmental damage

Recognised international crimes under the Rome Statute: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and crime of aggression

subtopics.title: Governance, Citizenship and Parliament
subtopics.summary: Draft Citizenship Rules amendments tighten declaration and passport-surrender norms for applicants from Pakistan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh, and India does not allow dual citizenship. A privilege notice moved in Rajya Sabha shows how MPs can allege a breach of parliamentary privilege. The Model Code of Conduct regulates elections, and the Supreme Court's One Case One Data initiative aims to integrate court data.
facts: Citizenship is covered under Part II (Articles 5 to 11) of the Constitution and is a Union List subject

Under the draft rules, a foreign passport must be surrendered within 15 days
Citizenship Act, 1955 lists five modes of acquisition: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory

subtopics.title: Economy, Agriculture and Employment
subtopics.summary: The RBI's Economic Capital Framework governs how it provides for risks and transfers surplus to the government, and the RBI Board approved a record transfer for FY 2025-26. The Index of Eight Core Industries and the Manufacturing PMI track industrial activity, with the PMI at 54.7 in April 2026. The Mission for Cotton Productivity aims at self-sufficiency in cotton by 2030-31, and the Centre raised the sugarcane Fair and Remunerative Price for the 2026-27 season.
facts: Economic Capital Framework (introduced in 2019) governs how the RBI provides for financial risks and transfers surplus to the Government of India
Surplus is transferred to the government only after Contingency Risk Buffer targets are met
RBI Board approved a record 2.86 lakh crore surplus transfer for FY 2025-26
Section 47 of the RBI Act, 1934 mandates that RBI profits be sent to the Centre
RBI surplus transfer typically averages around 0.5% of GDP
Eight core industries: coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement and electricity (base year 2011-12)
Index of Eight Core Industries grew 1.7% in April 2026; core industries carry a 40.27% weight in the Index of Industrial Production

Bt cotton is the only GM crop approved by GEAC for commercial cultivation in India

subtopics.title: Governance, Statistics and Panchayats
subtopics.summary: This subtopic covers the Panchayat Advancement Index 2.0, which grades rural local bodies on a composite score, and the 2025 National Panchayat Awards. It also covers the ASUSE survey of unincorporated enterprises, and the Public Accounts Committee that reviews government expenditure.
facts: PAI 2.0 was released by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj for FY 2023-24 and covers Gram Panchayats and Traditional Local Bodies.

Front Runner (A) covers scores of 75-89 and Performer (B) covers scores of 60-74.
Aspirant (C) covers scores of 40-59 and Beginner (D) covers scores below 40.

Tripura had the highest share of Front Runners among top performers, followed by Kerala and Odisha.
No Panchayat reached the Achiever category in PAI 2.0.
ASUSE 2025 covered the reference period Jan-Dec 2025, as MoSPI replaced the earlier Oct-Sep cycle with a calendar year.
National Panchayat Awards 2025 went to 42 Panchayats from 17 States and UTs, with Karnataka winning the most (6).
The Public Accounts Committee has 22 members (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha) and was first constituted in 1921.

subtopics.title: Environment and Space Missions
subtopics.summary: MARS is a satellite-based system that detects major methane leaks, and it is being widened to coal mines and waste facilities. SMILE is a joint mission that images how the solar wind interacts with Earth's magnetosphere and ionosphere, helping explain how Earth is shielded from harmful solar radiation.
facts: MARS (Methane Alert and Response System) is a satellite-based system designed to detect and help mitigate major methane leaks.
MARS was launched at COP27 (Sharm el-Sheikh) in 2022 and was developed under UNEP's International Methane Emissions Observatory.
MARS is expanding to coal mines and waste facilities; earlier it focused only on the oil and gas sector.
Methane has much greater short-term warming potential than carbon dioxide.
China, the United States and India rank among the world's largest methane emitters.
The Global Methane Pledge aims to cut global methane emissions by 30% by 2030 compared with 2020 levels; India is not a formal member.
SMILE was launched by ESA and the Chinese Academy of Sciences aboard a Vega-C rocket from French Guiana.
SMILE stands for Solar Wind Magnetosphere Ionosphere Link Explorer.
SMILE provides simultaneous X-ray and ultraviolet imaging of Earth's magnetosphere.
SMILE helps explain how Earth is protected from harmful solar radiation.

subtopics.title: Regional Groupings: SCO and IORA
subtopics.summary: The SCO is a Eurasian grouping that works to counter terrorism, separatism and extremism, and it gives India access to Central Asia's energy and trade. IORA is a cooperation body for countries bordering the Indian Ocean, and India chairs it for 2025-2027.
facts: SCO emerged from the Shanghai Five (1996) and became the SCO in 2001 after Uzbekistan joined.
The SCO's core objective is regional cooperation to counter terrorism, separatism and extremism.
SCO accounts for about 30% of global GDP and about 40% of the world population.
SCO has 10 members, including India (joined 2017) and four Central Asian nations.
The Council of Heads of States is the SCO's supreme decision-making body, and RATS is based in Tashkent.
The SCO secretariat is in Beijing, and its official languages are Russian and Chinese.
IORA was established in 1997; its vision originated during Nelson Mandela's 1995 visit to India.
IORA has 23 Member States and 12 Dialogue Partners, with its secretariat in Ebene (Mauritius).
IORA cooperation areas include maritime safety and security, fisheries management and disaster risk management.
The Indian Ocean Dialogue was launched in 2013 in Perth; India hosted editions in 2014, 2019 and 2021.

subtopics.title: Anniversaries and Historical Episodes
subtopics.summary: Three historical episodes are tied to recent anniversaries: the Korean War of 1950-53, the Komagata Maru voyage of 1914, and Sikkim's integration with India in 1975. Each shows how wars, migration restrictions or treaties shaped the status of a region or its people.
facts: Japanese occupation of Korea lasted from 1910 to 1945; North and South Korea were established in 1948.
North Korean troops crossed the 38th Parallel on 25 June 1950, and the UN Security Council condemned the invasion.
The Korean Armistice Agreement was signed on 27 July 1953, leading to a ceasefire without a peace treaty.
India chaired the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission and deployed the Custodian Force India for prisoners unwilling to return.
The Komagata Maru (Guru Nanak Jahaz), chartered by Gurdit Singh, carried 376 Indian passengers to Canada in 1914.
Canada's Continuous Journey Regulation (1908) required direct travel from the country of origin; only 24 passengers were allowed to disembark.
After the ship returned to India, British authorities tried to deport passengers at Budge Budge, and troops opened fire.

quizzes.title: UAE Visit Outcomes Check
quizzes.passage:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to the United Arab Emirates focused on energy security, defence, technology and investment. Energy was a central theme, with an Indian strategic reserves company signing a memorandum of understanding with Abu Dhabi National Oil Company for strategic collaboration. Talks also covered storing crude oil at Fujairah under India's Overseas Strategic Reserve Framework. Separately, Indian Oil Corporation and ADNOC signed a strategic collaboration agreement on LPG supply security, and a long-term LPG sale agreement was under consideration.

On defence and maritime matters, the framework for a Strategic Defence Partnership was advanced. A memorandum between Cochin Shipyard and Drydocks World aims to establish a ship repair cluster at Vadinar. Cooperation also includes offshore fabrication under the Maritime Development Fund Scheme.

In technology, a term sheet was signed for setting up supercomputing clusters, linked to India's AI Mission and a partnership between C-DAC and G42. Investment was also on the agenda, as two institutions agreed to explore investments in India's infrastructure sector.

Taken together, these outcomes show how India's partnership with the UAE now extends well beyond trade into petroleum security, shipbuilding, artificial intelligence and infrastructure finance. Several arrangements were signed, while others remain at the stage of proposals or discussions.

quizzes.title: OPEC and the UAE Exit: MCQ Set
quizzes.passage: Oil-producing countries have long coordinated their output so that crude prices do not swing too sharply. When prices fall too low, exporters that depend on petroleum revenue lose income, and when supply runs ahead of demand, the market can become oversupplied. Recently the United Arab Emirates announced that it would leave the producer group and its wider alliance with other oil exporters, a move seen as a major geopolitical shift. Collective decisions by the group have traditionally helped it shape global oil prices, so the departure of a large producer may reduce that influence. Member countries have different national priorities and economic needs, which can make agreement on output levels difficult even within a well-established group. Such limits are usually set by agreement among members. Output quotas were one reason behind the exit, because they limited how fully the UAE could use its expanding capacity. The booklet also points to growing competition among producers, including rivalry between the UAE and a major regional neighbour. The episode matters for importing countries such as India as well, since lower prices could ease their import bills while greater volatility could make long-term budgeting harder. Taken together, the exit shows how energy markets, regional politics and national economic goals are closely linked.

quizzes.passage: One reason given for the UAE's exit is that output limits set through the producer group kept it from using its growing production capacity in full. The country's outlook looks ahead to a time when global oil demand may peak and then decline gradually. Its present approach is to earn strong oil revenues in the near term while preparing for a longer-term shift to renewable energy. Those revenues are intended to help fund growth in artificial intelligence and data centres, supporting a more diversified economy. Friction within the producer group over production policy has been long-standing, and rivalry between the UAE and a regional neighbour over economic and political influence has intensified. Infrastructure also adds flexibility: an inland pipeline in the UAE carries crude from oil fields to a coastal terminal on the Gulf of Oman, which helps exporters when shipping routes face disruption risks. For India, which imports a large share of its crude, lower oil prices would reduce import costs and ease inflation pressure, while a move away from group restrictions could allow direct bilateral deals. The booklet also notes that rising volatility could complicate long-term energy budgeting. Taken together, these developments show how energy, security and economic strategy are tied together in the Gulf.

quizzes.passage:
Exam malpractice damages more than one test. When the credibility of the system falls, the market value of degrees and merit rankings can fall with it. Re-conducting a compromised examination also places a heavy financial burden on government institutions, and large-scale cheating makes parents and students lose confidence in educational fairness. Students are hit too. Cancellations delay admissions, and honest candidates face stress and demotivation.

After the NEET-UG 2024 controversy, the Ministry of Education set up a high-level committee. Its major recommendations address the functioning of the testing agency and the way examinations are conducted. The panel proposed limiting the role of the National Testing Agency to entrance examinations, and it suggested a technology-enabled authentication system. It also called for governance reforms through an empowered governing body, and for more secure examination centres. Over time, the panel suggested that future entrance examinations move gradually towards computer adaptive testing.

quizzes.title: Public Examination Act check

The Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act 2024 was framed to curb paper leaks, organised cheating and manipulation in recruitment and entrance examinations. It covers a broad range of unfair means. Leaking question papers or answer keys, impersonating a candidate, and giving unauthorised assistance during an examination are all covered. So are tampering with computer systems or networks, conducting fake examinations, and manipulating merit lists or official documents.

Punishments depend on the offence and on the person responsible. Individuals who are found guilty can face imprisonment as well as monetary penalties, and organised malpractice carries monetary penalties as well. Service providers who run examinations can be fined and barred from conducting examinations for a fixed period. Organised crimes are punished separately under the Act.

Offences under the Act are serious. Investigations are carried out by senior police officers, and the Central Government has the power to shift an investigation to a central agency where needed. Together, these provisions treat examination fraud as a serious crime rather than a minor lapse.

quizzes.title: Court ruling: legal reasoning
quizzes.passage: The Madhya Pradesh High Court has ruled on the Bhojshala - Kamal Maula Complex, a medieval monument in Dhar, Madhya Pradesh. Relying on findings from a survey by the Archaeological Survey of India, the court declared the complex a Hindu temple dedicated to Goddess Vagdevi, another name for Saraswati. In the same ruling, the court quashed an earlier ASI order that had allowed shared worship at the site. The bench held that the Places of Worship Act, 1991 could not be applied here, because the site is a protected monument under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958. The freeze on religious character in the Act does not extend to such monuments. The Muslim side had relied on a proclamation issued by the princely State of Dhar in 1935. The bench rejected this reliance, noting that the Government of India Act, 1935, on which the proclamation rested, had not been enforced until a later date. The case was treated as a writ petition seeking enforcement of the fundamental right to worship, unlike the Babri Masjid dispute, which was a title suit about ownership. To balance the rights of both communities, the court directed the State Government to consider applications for allotting alternative land within Dhar for a mosque or prayer site.

quizzes.title: Places of Worship Act: key details
quizzes.passage: The Places of Worship Act, 1991 was passed by a Congress government to protect the religious identity of places of worship. Its central aim is to keep the religious character of each place as it stood on Independence Day. The Act prohibits converting a place of worship from one religious denomination to another, whether between or within denominations. It terminates pending legal proceedings about religious character conversions that took place before the cut-off, while allowing new cases about changes made after it. Violating the Act attracts imprisonment and fines. The Act exempts ancient monuments protected under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, and it does not cover the Ayodhya dispute and related legal proceedings. Critics argue that the Act limits judicial review, weakening constitutional checks and balances. Others say that it violates the right to freedom of religion and treats communities differently, undermining equality. Critics also argue that the Independence Day cut-off ignores historical injustices and earlier encroachments. The Supreme Court, in its verdict on the Ayodhya dispute, said that the Act upholds secular values and prohibits retrogression. Its supporters say the Act ensures the preservation of religious sites and their character, instilling confidence in all communities. Together, these points explain why the Act remains a contested law.

quizzes.passage: The Supreme Court of India sits at the apex of the country's judicial system and is described as the final interpreter and guardian of the Constitution. It began functioning in the early months of 1950 and took over the role of the highest court of appeal that the British Privy Council had earlier held. The Court's strength is not fixed in the Constitution; it can be changed by law, and it has grown over the years from its original size. The Union Cabinet has now approved a bill to enlarge the bench further. The government's aim is to tackle the Court's growing caseload, which has led to a massive backlog of cases. A bigger bench is expected to speed up the disposal of cases and improve timely delivery of justice in constitutional and civil matters. It would also make it easier to constitute constitution benches, special benches and larger benches for important cases. Such an expansion is seen as a way of strengthening judicial capacity. The amendment bill must pass through both Houses of Parliament before it can take effect, and it also needs the President's assent. Judges of the Court are appointed by the President, and the Constitution sets out the organisation, independence, jurisdiction and powers of the Court in detail.

quizzes.title: Appointment, Tenure and Removal Facts
quizzes.passage: Judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President, and the Constitution lays down the qualifications a person must have before appointment. A candidate must be a citizen of India and must meet one of several experience-based or distinguished-jurist criteria. Once in office, a judge does not serve a fixed term. Instead, the judge continues until reaching a set retirement age, and may also choose to leave earlier by writing to the President. The Constitution provides a formal route for removal, which is demanding. Removal is permitted only on the grounds of proven misbehaviour or incapacity. A special law governs the procedure, and the same process applies to judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Courts. Several judges have faced removal motions in Parliament, and in some cases the motion failed or the judge resigned before the process was complete. The question of who should decide appointments has been debated for decades, and Court rulings have repeatedly reshaped the process. Consultation between the Chief Justice and other senior judges sits at the heart of that debate. These disputes show how closely appointments and removals are linked to judicial independence.
